title: Hashimoto's encephalopathy: Follow‐up data from neuropsychology, lumbar puncture, and FDG‐PET
case_prompt:
A 66-year-old man with no prior neurologic disease was referred for evaluation of subacute cognitive and neurologic symptoms. Over the preceding weeks, he developed memory impairment, progressive speech difficulties, dizziness, fluctuating awareness, balance problems, apraxia, twitching of the extremities, mood changes, and visual hallucinations. On examination, he had mild aphasia and dysarthria, bilateral resting tremor, truncal instability, myoclonus, severe bilateral apraxia, and dysdiadochokinesia; the Mini–Mental State Examination score was 25/30. Neuropsychological testing revealed a dysexecutive/subcortical cognitive profile, fulfilling formal criteria for dementia.

Cerebral CT excluded subdural hematoma, and supplemental MRI was normal. Chest radiography and full-body PET showed no extra-cerebral malignancy; paraneoplastic antibodies in blood were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated elevated protein and a mild pleocytosis; biomarkers for Alzheimer’s disease (Aß42, F-tau, P-tau) were negative. Testing for Lyme disease was negative. Brain ^18F-FDG–PET showed globally decreased cortical glucose metabolism, interpreted as more consistent with metabolic or toxic effects than with a neurodegenerative process.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. CNS infection — “The patient was tested negative for Lyme disease.”  
2. Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis — “Chest X‐Ray and full‐body‐PET showed no signs of extra‐cerebral malignancy. Also, test results for paraneoplastic antibodies in blood were normal.”  
3. Alzheimer's disease — “There were negative biomarkers for Alzheimer's dementia (Aß42, F‐tau; P‐tau) in the cerebrospinal fluid.”  
4. Vascular causes (e.g., subdural hematoma) — “Cerebral CT had previously excluded subdural hematoma.”  
5. Connective tissue disorders (e.g., systemic lupus) — “Screening blood tests for connective tissue disorders were also normal.”
